articles.title: Telonia – Categories
articles.excerpt: Classification of Telonia into three categories: pastoral demons, vrykolakes, and kallikantzaroi.

content.value: The telonia are divided into three categories:

Those similar to pastoral demons, called like them chamodrakia or smerdakia. These appear as fire or emit sparks, they mock night-wanderers or harm them by throwing stones, as other demons do. They trouble and torment them in various ways. They also mount livestock, like pastoral demons, and bring destruction upon them. According to the Cretan tradition in question, being fully assimilated to demons, they have black wings and torment people as other demons do.
Second, the telonia identified with the vrykolakes, corresponding to those who died prematurely in ancient beliefs — the night-wandering attendants of Hecate.
Third, the telonia identified with the Kallikantzaroi, which are infants conceived and born in sin during the Twelve Days.
Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, N. G. Politis – Traditions, Part B, 1904 – p. 1236

articles.title: Pyrgos of Samos – The Demonic Child
articles.excerpt: Account of a man who carries a demonic child near Pyrgos on Samos.

content.value: A man on his way to Pyrgos passed through the Kakavorema ravine and there found a small child alone. Thinking the child had been abandoned by its mother, the man took it with him and wrapped it in clothes. The child had not stopped crying throughout the journey, and the man stroked it and repeated: "Hush, my baby, hush, my baby."

Just as they arrived outside Pyrgos, the child suddenly cried out "Hush, my baby, hush, my baby!" and, bursting into flames, vanished from the man's arms. The man realized it had been a telonion and, returning home, recounted the terrifying incident.

articles.title: Telonia of Tinos
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk narrative about apparent meteorological phenomena and their supernatural interpretations

content.value: When a sudden whirlwind arises, telonia fall like a mist, like trembling things, into the sea. They chase the light, and lightning chases them. First they go to the mastheads, and you would think they were stars in the sky.

Then they come down to the rigging. Then they fill the ropes. You hold them in your hands and they produce little fires, soft things. Then we light a fire, throw incense, cense the air, put out the lights so they leave.
When a dog barks, or a pig, they flee; but the dog burrows in and no matter how hard you beat it, it will not bark.

articles.title: The Telonia – Athens
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk practice for dealing with demonic phenomena in maritime tradition

content.value: When telonia appear on a ship, if they have pigs aboard, they turn them and pull them to make them squeal. In this way they drive off the demons, since pigs too are diabolical.
And all the sailors strip naked and slap their buttocks.

articles.title: The Telonia of Crete
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk belief about unbaptized dead infants who transform into demonic entities

content.value: Babies who die unbaptized become little demons with black wings.
And as they fly through the air, they curse the priest who left them unbaptized, they stone passers-by, and they torment them, as other demons do.
If someone passes at night — especially at midnight — through the place where they are buried or left, they hear them crying and see sparks and fires.
